cases.abstract: Accepting a long input does not establish that a language model can use evidence throughout it. We diagnose this distinction with multi-document question answering and synthetic key-value retrieval, varying context length and the position of the relevant item while preserving the required answer. In the evaluated question-answering models, placing the answer passage in the middle generally lowers accuracy relative to placing it at either end; some settings fall below answering without documents, even though the answer passage is present. Extended-context variants perform almost identically to their shorter-context counterparts when both can accommodate the same input. Repeating the query before and after the context largely eliminates synthetic lookup failures but leaves the question-answering position pattern intact, showing that successful token retrieval need not entail effective evidence use. Encoder-decoder models are less position-sensitive within their training-time context lengths, yet also develop middle-context degradation on longer inputs. In a standard retrieval pipeline, reader accuracy saturates while retrieval recall continues to rise. These converging tests identify evidence access and use, rather than accepted context length or answer availability alone, as a bottleneck in the evaluated question-answering settings.
cases.methods: Moving the answer passage while holding the question and available documents fixed tests whether evidence availability is enough for successful answering. The study uses 2,655 NaturalQuestions-Open queries whose annotated long answers are paragraphs. Each prompt contains one annotated answer passage and relevance-ranked distractors filtered to exclude annotated answers. Placing the answer passage at different positions in 10-, 20-, and 30-document contexts tests position sensitivity; changing the distractor count tests the effect of added context without changing the target answer. Closed-book prompts establish performance without supplied evidence, while an oracle prompt supplies only the answer passage. A complementary task uses unique random UUID key-value pairs to reduce linguistic confounds and test exact lookup. Both tasks use greedy decoding and score inclusion of a correct answer or value. Repeating the query before and after the data probes whether allowing earlier tokens to be contextualized with the query changes these two tasks differently.
cases.results: Query repetition distinguishes an exact-lookup failure from a broader difficulty using retrieved text. With 300 UUID key-value pairs, GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) achieves 100% accuracy when the query appears on both sides of the data, whereas its worst-position accuracy with the query only afterward is 45.6%. In multi-document question answering, however, repetition leaves the positional pattern largely unchanged: it slightly helps when evidence comes first and slightly hurts other placements. Query-aware prompting therefore does not provide a general remedy for the tested evidence-use problem. Some GPT-3.5-Turbo settings with 20 or 30 documents fall below its 56.1% closed-book accuracy despite containing an answer passage, so supplying evidence among distractors can be worse than supplying none. In the separate retrieval-pipeline study, adding documents beyond 20 produces only marginal reader gains while retrieval recall continues to improve. Together, these comparisons show that successful lookup and higher retrieval recall do not, by themselves, establish effective question answering.
cases.notes: Sections 2.3 and 4.2 support the diagnostic sequence: unchanged answer availability, position-sensitive QA, and a task-dependent query-placement intervention. Section 5 tests whether increasing recall improves reader performance. Kept the closed-book failure to convey the practical consequence; architecture findings remain conditional observations, not causal explanations. Omitted the unspecified scale of the reported decline exceeding 20%. Distractor filtering excludes annotated answers, not every reasonable answer; the unambiguous-question check preserved the trends.

cases.abstract: Retrieved text can be relevant to a query without supporting the claims in an answer. SELF-RAG makes that distinction part of generation: a language model learns when to retrieve and uses predicted relevance, support, and utility to select sentence continuations. A critic trained on GPT-4 feedback annotates instruction-output pairs offline; the generator learns text and reflection tokens together with a standard next-token objective. At inference, it supplies its own assessments, allowing retrieval frequency and evidential emphasis to be adjusted without retraining or calling the critic. Zero-shot evaluation of 7B and 13B Llama 2 models covers six tasks spanning factual questions, closed-set decisions, biographies, and cited long-form answers. With the same five supplied ASQA documents, SELF-RAG 7B achieves 66.9% citation precision, compared with 5.0% for Llama2-FT 7B, trained on the same instruction-output pairs but using retrieval only at inference. However, its str-em correctness is lower, and increasing the support weight raises citation precision while lowering MAUVE, the reported fluency metric. The evidence supports improved attribution and adjustable tradeoffs, rather than a uniform gain across response qualities.
cases.methods: SELF-RAG learns evidence judgments alongside response text so that a separate critic is unnecessary at inference. During data preparation, a Llama 2 critic trained on GPT-4 reflection labels decides whether a target segment needs retrieval, labels passage relevance, and assesses support for that segment; response utility is judged independently of the passages. The generator learns from these augmented examples using next-token prediction, with retrieved passage tokens excluded from the loss. At inference, it produces a candidate sentence and critique tokens for each retrieved passage. Segment-level beam search ranks continuations using generation probability plus a weighted sum of normalized probabilities for favorable relevance, support, and utility labels, rather than simply accepting the top retrieved passage. The support weight can therefore change which continuation is selected, while a threshold on the normalized retrieval-token probability controls whether evidence is requested. These operations make learned assessments adjustable selection criteria without another training run.
cases.results: SELF-RAG improves ASQA attribution without uniformly improving answer correctness. Using the same five supplied passages, its 7B model achieves citation precision and recall of 66.9% and 67.8%, versus 5.0% and 7.5% for Llama2-FT 7B, trained on the same instruction-output pairs with retrieval added only at inference. Yet str-em correctness is 30.0 versus 31.0. The contrast concerns how available evidence is incorporated, not access to more test-time documents. In a separate ablation with 50,000 training examples and 150 sampled ASQA questions, training on the top retrieved passage without reflection tokens yields str-em of 18.1, compared with 32.1 for SELF-RAG. The ablation changes passage handling as well as reflection supervision, so it supports the combined configuration rather than isolating critique tokens. Test-time controls expose further tradeoffs: increasing the support weight improves citation precision but reduces MAUVE, while raising the retrieval threshold reduces retrieval frequency and causes greater accuracy deterioration on PopQA than PubHealth. Thus, stronger attribution and less retrieval are choices with distinct costs, not interchangeable improvements in overall answer quality.
cases.notes: Table 2 anchors the attribution-versus-correctness contrast under shared ASQA documents and instruction-output pairs; it does not support superiority on every metric. Main training uses 150,000 pairs. Figure 3a ablations instead use 50,000 pairs, with ASQA restricted to 150 sampled instances. The no-critic variant changes passage handling as well as reflection supervision, preventing attribution to critique tokens alone. Figures 3b and 3c support adjustable tradeoffs, not cost-free factuality or retrieval reductions. MAUVE remains the reported fluency metric; reflection predictions are not guarantees of evidential support.
